newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE-Time ticking away for Brazil's reforming president.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Time ticking away for Brazil's reforming president.

text.p: A few months ago, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, basking in the prospect of re-election, looked set to meet his promise of transforming Brazil by pushing long-awaited reforms through Congress.

Now, it seems the "reform president" will have to win an unprecedented second term next year before he can apply the finishing touches to his inflation-slashing Real Plan which turns three years old on July 1.
"When the re-election bill went through, I was one of those who thought Fernando Henrique would be very strong. Well, it just hasn't happened," said political analyst Ricardo Pedreira.
STILL TRYING TO WAKE A SLEEPING GIANT
Cardoso took office in January 1995, repeating the familiar pledges of his predecessors to turn Latin America's sleeping giant into an economic powerhouse.

His success in cutting Brazil's once-rampant inflation to single digits last year and the $5 billion privatisation of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Vale begun in May have gone a long way to upholding his credentials as a dynamic moderniser.

But to bury once and for all Brazil's stigma as the perennial country of the future, Cardoso has yet to tackle obstinate structural problems -- an inefficient and overstaffed civil service and a pensions system nosediving into debt.

It seemed to most observers that he would finally get his chance earlier this year. In January, the lower house of Congress approved a controversial bill allowing the president to stand for a second term, ending a century-old ban on re-election.

Cardoso was already riding high in opinion polls and instantly became the favourite to win the 1998 presidential race. Cartoonists depicted him as an emperor bedecked in ermine robes and surrounded by scraping lawmakers.
RE-ELECTION BILL MEANS EARLY CAMPAIGN START

But far from strengthening Cardoso's hand, the re-election bill, which is now law, has prompted an early, and increasingly unruly, start to campaigning for the October 1998 presidential, congressional and state governorship elections.

Even Cardoso's supporters say the civil service and pension reforms must be approved by September, when the government's fragile, multi-party alliance in Congress is expected to unravel amid election fever. Otherwise, the reforms will have to wait for a few more years yet.

"If we give up now, the reforms might not be approved until the year 2000. The next Congress won't necessarily be any more dynamic than this one," said Roberto Brant, a member of the Chamber of Deputies and a friend of the president.
Without reforms, Brazil has little chance of breaking with its underachieving past.

Many states spend 80 percent of receipts on their own payrolls, leaving little for their ailing hospitals and schools. The pension system, which allows many civil servants to retire by 45, is heading for a one-billion-dollar deficit in 1997, a shortfall expected to rise sharply.
Everyone agrees the situation has to change. But the reforms, which have already been watered down to placate opponents, have been stuck in Congress for more than two years.

The government blames cosy relations between a powerful civil service lobby and a self-serving parliament. Disgruntled lawmakers accuse the government of failing to keep its promises. commentators ask why Cardoso, who got his re-election bill approved in just a few months, cannot speed things up.
PRESIDENT REGRETS "REFORMS OR NOTHING" APPROACH
The president himself has questioned the wisdom of placing much of the thrust of his government on two reform bills.

In a recent television interview, Cardoso was asked if he had any regrets. "I would have placed less emphasis on the idea that it was reforms or nothing. People have the idea the government is tied to Congress," he replied.

The president is clearly disappointed. With the reforms approved, Brazil could have begun dismantling its strict monetary constraints to double its currently sluggish economic growth rate of about three percent a year.
Cardoso would then have gone into next year's elections on the crest of a wave of optimism.

But few believe the reform delays mean an imminent collapse of Brazil's cautious economic recovery. Stock markets have turned a blind eye to the political intrigues of Brasilia, chalking up spectacular gains of 80 percent this year alone.

Analysts say privatisation of the massive telecommunications and power industries will bring in at least $60 billion over the next few years, guaranteeing the government a steady supply of dollars to cover its stubborn external accounts deficits.
FOUR MORE YEARS?

Nor are there many storm clouds for Cardoso on the political horizon. Claims in May that lawmakers were paid to vote for the re-election bill took the shine off his spotless reputation. But no one can see any serious challenger threatening his re-election bid.

His success in keeping inflation down for three years has not only kept him high in opinion polls but has denied would-be opponents the scope for attacking his policies, said Thomas Skidmore, a professor of Brazilian politics at Brown University in Rhode Island.
"Fernando Henrique is going to become the indispensable man," Skidmore said during a recent television interview. "He can brand his opponents as the friends of inflation...It's going to be easy."
